items.readable_text:
Content:
The scalar projection of a vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto another vector [MATH: \mathbf{b}] is the distance that the vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] extends in the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
For example, consider two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}] shown below. Suppose we know that [MATH: |\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2] and that the angle between the vectors is [MATH: \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/64af6629c431159c6711f4513a638ed2]

Content:
To illustrate the projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] along [MATH: \mathbf{b},] consider the point [MATH: P] on the line that contains [MATH: \mathbf{b}] with [MATH: AP \perp \mathbf{b},] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/afba77446d85db03d103433487bec49b]

Content:
The length [MATH: OP] is called the scalar projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] (or the component of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] along [MATH: \mathbf{b}]). It is denoted as [MATH: \text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a},] and we can compute it using cosine in [MATH: \triangle OPA] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: comp_{b}a|= OP; =|a|\cos θ; = 2\cos ((π)/(4)); = 2 ⋅ (sqrt(2))/(2); = sqrt(2)]

Content:
This formula is the general definition of the scalar projection:

Content:
[MATH: \text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}= |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta]

items.readable_text:
Content:
The scalar projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] can be negative. This happens when the vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] extends in the direction opposite to that of [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a246cb0b361184d4b0f402de21f2919c]

Content:
For example, consider two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b},] where it is known that

Content:
[MATH: |\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2, \qquad \theta = 135^\circ.]

Content:
Notice that the angle [MATH: \theta] between the vectors is obtuse.

Content:
Computing the scalar projection of [MATH: \mathbf a] onto [MATH: \mathbf b] using the formula, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: comp_{b}a|=|a|\cos θ; = 2\cos (135^{∘}); = 2 ⋅ (− (sqrt(2))/(2)); = − sqrt(2).]

Content:
In general, if [MATH: 90^\circ < \theta \leq 180^\circ,] then [MATH: \cos\theta <0] and the scalar projection will be negative.

items.readable_text:
Content:
We have been using the following formula for the scalar projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}= |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta]

Content:
However, sometimes we are not given the angle between two vectors. In such cases, we can solve for [MATH: \cos \theta] in terms of the dot product:

Content:
[MATH: a ⋅ b|=|a||b|\cos θ; \cos θ|= (a ⋅ b)/(|a||b|)]

Content:
Substituting this into our original formula, we get

Content:
[MATH: comp_{b}a|=|a|\cos θ; =|a|⋅ (a ⋅ b)/(|a||b|); = (a ⋅ b)/(|b|).]

Content:
Therefore, another general formula for the scalar projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] is

Content:
[MATH: comp_{b}a|= (a ⋅ b)/(|b|).]

Notice that if two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}] are perpendicular, then the scalar projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] (or [MATH: \mathbf{b}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{a}]) is equal to [MATH: 0.]

Content:
For example, consider the following illustration. Notice that, since [MATH: \mathbf{a} \perp \mathbf{b},] the vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] doesn't extend in the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{b}] at all. So, the scalar projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] is [MATH: 0.]

Furthermore, we have the following fact:

Content:
> If [MATH: \mathbf{a}] is a nonzero vector, its scalar projection onto another nonzero vector [MATH: \mathbf{b}] equals [MATH: 0] if and only if the vectors are perpendicular.

For example, consider two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b},] where it is known that

Content:
[MATH: |\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2, \qquad \theta = 135^\circ.]

Content:
Notice that the angle [MATH: \theta] between the vectors is obtuse.

Content:
Computing the scalar projection of [MATH: \mathbf a] onto [MATH: \mathbf b] using the formula, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: comp_{b}a|=|a|\cos θ; = 2\cos (135^{∘}); = 2 ⋅ (− (sqrt(2))/(2)); = − sqrt(2).]

Content:
In general, if [MATH: 90^\circ < \theta \leq 180^\circ,] then [MATH: \cos\theta <0] and the scalar projection will be negative.

EXPLANATION

[MATH: comp_{b}a|=|a|\cos θ; = 13\cos ((2π)/(3)); = 13 ⋅ (− (1)/(2)); = − (13)/(2).]

Item 6 — Tutorial: Deriving a General Formula

Content:
We have been using the following formula for the scalar projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}= |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta]

Content:
However, sometimes we are not given the angle between two vectors. In such cases, we can solve for [MATH: \cos \theta] in terms of the dot product:

Content:
[MATH: a ⋅ b|=|a||b|\cos θ; \cos θ|= (a ⋅ b)/(|a||b|)]

Content:
Substituting this into our original formula, we get

Content:
[MATH: comp_{b}a|=|a|\cos θ; =|a|⋅ (a ⋅ b)/(|a||b|); = (a ⋅ b)/(|b|).]

Content:
Therefore, another general formula for the scalar projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] is

Content:
[MATH: comp_{b}a|= (a ⋅ b)/(|b|).]

Item 7 — Example: Calculating a Scalar Projection Using Components

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: \mathbf{a}=\langle 3,3,-1 \rangle] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}=\langle 2,-7,0 \rangle.] Find the scalar projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

[MATH: comp_{b}a|= (a ⋅ b)/(|b|); = (a_{x}b_{x} + a_{y}b_{y} + a_{z}b_{z})/(sqrt(b_{x}^{2} + b_{y}^{2} + b_{z}^{2})); = (3 ⋅ 2 + 3 ⋅ (− 7) + (− 1) ⋅ 0)/(sqrt(2^{2} + (− 7)^{2} + 0^{2})); = − (15)/(sqrt(53)).]

Item 10 — Tutorial: Projecting Perpendicular Vectors

Content:
Notice that if two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}] are perpendicular, then the scalar projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] (or [MATH: \mathbf{b}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{a}]) is equal to [MATH: 0.]

Content:
For example, consider the following illustration. Notice that, since [MATH: \mathbf{a} \perp \mathbf{b},] the vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] doesn't extend in the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{b}] at all. So, the scalar projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] is [MATH: 0.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/343c7ce96cd3598d0a81cd8f5e38ae9f]

Content:
Furthermore, we have the following fact:

Content:
> If [MATH: \mathbf{a}] is a nonzero vector, its scalar projection onto another nonzero vector [MATH: \mathbf{b}] equals [MATH: 0] if and only if the vectors are perpendicular.

Item 11 — Example: Projecting a Vector Onto a Perpendicular Vector

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: [0; 0; 1]] and [MATH: [2; − 4; 0]] Find the scalar projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

[MATH: comp_{b}a|= (a ⋅ b)/(|b|); = (a_{x}b_{x} + a_{y}b_{y} + c_{z}b_{z})/(sqrt(b_{x}^{2} + b_{y}^{2} + b_{z}^{2})); = (0 ⋅ 2 + 0 ⋅ (− 4) + 1 ⋅ 0)/(sqrt(2^{2} + (− 4)^{2} + 0^{2})); = (0)/(sqrt(2^{2} + (− 4)^{2} + 0^{2})); = 0.]
